native component FlatString

import String.{maxLeafSize, concatAndBalanceIfNecessary, CatString, spaces}
import Stream.{...}

export FlatString


private language="java"
private package="com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.prim"

lineSeparator: String = LineSeparator()

private natLineSeparator(): String = builtinPrimitive(
            "com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.stringOps.lineSeparator")

private LineSeparator(): String =do
    ignore(FlatString); (* This initializes the constructor for FlatString
                   before its type is used (in the next line). *)
    natLineSeparator()
  end

object FlatString extends { String, DelegatedIndexed⟦Char, ZZ32⟧ }
    getter size() : ZZ32 =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.simpleConcatenate.nativeStrlen")
    getter asExprString() : String =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.stringOps.asExprString")
    getter asFlatString(): String = self
    getter asString(): String = self
    getter asDebugString(): String = asDebugStringIndented(0)
    getter depth():ZZ32 = 0

    (* With the help of trait DelegatedIndex, this defines our generate method *)
    getter generator() : Generator⟦Char⟧ =
        self.indices.map⟦Char⟧(fn (i:ZZ32):Char ⇒ self.get(i))

    getter isBalanced():Boolean = true
    getter isAlmostBalanced():Boolean = true
    getter isExtremelyUnbalanced():Boolean = false

    balanced():String = self

    opr |self| : ZZ32 =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.simpleConcatenate.nativeStrlen")

    uncheckedSubstring(r1: Range⟦ZZ32⟧) : String = do
    (* We could build a subString node here, but not until everything is working,
        because that will introduce
       SubString objects into code that may still expect FlatStrings.
       As written, this method always answers a FlatString.
       In any case, the FlatString object supports substring without copying*)
        assert((r1 ∩ self.bounds).isEmpty, r1.isEmpty,
                    "Empty substring of non-empty string")
        if r1.isEmpty then ""
        else self.javaSubstr(r1.left.get, r1.right.get + 1)    (* Java substr's endIndex is one past the last character *)
        end
    end

    opr =(self, other: FlatString): Boolean =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.prim.FlatString$Eq")
    opr <(self, other: FlatString): Boolean = self.cmp(other) < 0
    opr <=(self, other: FlatString): Boolean = self.cmp(other) ≤ 0
    opr >(self, other: FlatString): Boolean = self.cmp(other) > 0
    opr >=(self, other: FlatString): Boolean = self.cmp(other) ≥ 0
    opr CMP(self, other: FlatString): TotalComparison =  self.cmp(other) CMP 0
    opr CMP(self, other:String):TotalComparison = INVERSE (other CMP self)
    opr CASE_INSENSITIVE_CMP(self, other:FlatString): TotalComparison =
      self.cicmp(other) CMP 0
    opr CASE_INSENSITIVE_CMP(self, other:String): TotalComparison = INVERSE (other CASE_INSENSITIVE_CMP self)

    (** get skips bounds checking. **)
    get(i:ZZ32): Char =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.stringOps.charAt")
    cmp(other:FlatString): ZZ32 =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.stringOps.compareTo")
    cicmp(other:FlatString): ZZ32 =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.stringOps.compareToIgnoreCase")
    javaSubstr(lo:ZZ32,hi:ZZ32): String =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.stringOps.javaSubstr")
    javaSubstr(lo:ZZ32): String = javaSubstr(lo, self.size)
    javaIndexOf(c:Char): ZZ32 =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.stringOps.indexOf")
    flatConcat(self, b:FlatString):String =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.simpleConcatenate.nativeConcatenate")
    flatConcat(self, b:Char):String =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.prim.FlatString$Concat")
    javaRegExpMatches(m:FlatString): Boolean =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.stringOps.javaRegExpMatches")
    javaRegExpSplit(m:FlatString, i:ZZ32): String =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.stringOps.javaRegExpSplit")

    indexOf(c:Char): Maybe⟦ZZ32⟧ = do
        i = javaIndexOf(c)
        if i = -1 then Nothing⟦ZZ32⟧ else Just⟦ZZ32⟧(i) end
      end

    verify():() = do
        assert(self.depth, 0, self)
    end

    asDebugStringIndented(indent: ZZ32): String =
        spaces(indent) || "J" |self| "/" self.depth ":" self

    opr ∈(c:Char, self): Boolean = self.javaIndexOf(c) ≠ -1

    rangeContains(r: Range⟦ZZ32⟧, c: Char):Boolean = self.javaIndexOf(c) ∈ self.bounds[r]

    (** The operator %||% with at least one String argument converts to string and
        concatenates **)
    opr ||(self, b:FlatString): String = do
        if b.isEmpty then self
        elif self.size + b.size > maxLeafSize then
             (* Since both self and b have depth 0, balancing can't be necessary *)
            CatString(self, b)
        else
            flatConcat(self, b)
        end
      end

    opr ||(self, b:String):String = do
        if self.isEmpty then b
        elif b.isEmpty then self
        elif self.size + b.size > maxLeafSize then
            concatAndBalanceIfNecessary(self, b)
        else
            typecase b.asFlatString of
                f:FlatString ⇒ flatConcat(self, f)
                f:String ⇒ concatAndBalanceIfNecessary(self, b)
            end
        end
    end

    opr ||(self, b:Char): String =
        if |self| ≥ maxLeafSize then
            concatAndBalanceIfNecessary(self, b.asString)
        else
            flatConcat(self, b)
        end

    splitWithOffsets():ZeroIndexed⟦(ZZ32, String)⟧ = Nothing⟦(ZZ32, String)⟧
    split():Generator⟦String⟧ = Nothing⟦String⟧

    writeOn(stream: WriteStream): () = stream.write(self)

end FlatString

end

## The row template

A row is one line of eight cells, `| # | claim | status | class | spec citation | reproducer | found by | notes / workaround |`, at most 1,200 characters, in the table of its topic section, in number order. A pipe inside a cell is written `\|`. (POSITIONS, "The gap ledger's form"; the proposal behind it is `explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/gap-ledger-archaeology.md`, section 4.)

- **#**: the row's number, the next free one when it is added; never reused, renumbered or given to another row. 148 is vacant.
- **claim**: at most 300 characters, whose first 150 name the defect or the capability: what fails or what holds, and where.
- **status**: exactly one word of seven, with no second status and nothing in brackets:
  - `POSITIVE-VERIFIED`: it works; it ran and its output is recorded.
  - `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED`: the specification settles it and the reproducer confirms it. A row with one half fixed stays `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED`, and its notes say which half is fixed.
  - `NEGATIVE-BOUNDED`: the failure reproduces; the mechanisms tried are named and are not exhaustive.
  - `CONTESTED`: unsettled; the notes say why.
  - `RETIRED`: a source's claim falsified here, kept so that it is not derived again.
  - `FIXED`: closed by a landed commit (`ledger.py close`): the claim's first sentence, the test as reproducer, notes `fixed HASH; full text: history, row N`.
  - `DUPLICATE`: a pointer (`ledger.py duplicate`), notes `duplicate of row M; full text: history, row N`.
- **class**: `kind (area)`; `—` only for `POSITIVE-VERIFIED` and `RETIRED`. The kind is one of `implementation gap`, `library gap vs spec`, `library bug`, `design limit`, `deliberate`, `typesetter`, `packaging`; the area one of `parser`, `walk`, `checker`, `codegen`, `runtime`, `library`, `prelude`, `specification`, `tests`, `tools`.
- **spec citation**: the `.tex` file and the section heading in quotes, as `basic/operators/juxtameaning.tex`, "Juxtaposition"; a line number only against `Specification-1.0-frozen/`; `silent` where the specification does not say.
- **reproducer**: one test (its name, or its path under the test folders; an `XXX` test while it is an expected failure) or one probe path from the repository root, at most 200 characters; `none` when nothing in the tree reproduces it, with the command and its output, or the probe's old path, in the notes.
- **found by**: the stream that found it (`climb batch 8 rung I`, `run-c3`, `apl rung 2`), at most 60 characters; no date and no role.
- **notes / workaround**: at most 700 characters: `siblings: N, M` first if there are any; the mechanism, with file:line and the commit it was true at; the workaround; for a closed row, `fixed HASH`.

A path under `explorations/` that is no longer in the tree is read from history: `git show $(git log -1 --diff-filter=D --format=%h -- PATH)^:PATH`.

### 5.5 What the sample shows

1. **A row's claim is not kept in step with its notes or the tree.** A batch fixes half of a row or changes its message. The note that says so is refused, or goes in after the history marker, and the claim keeps the old statement. Cases: 307, 330, 441, 539, 665, 701, 726 and 782. No command corrects an open row's claim (`records.md`, "Three limits of `ledger.py`"). This is the main source of the consistency failures.
2. **Fixed but open.** 642 and 577 are fixed and stay open only because `close` has no route for them: a `CONTESTED` row, and a test outside the test folders (`explorations/coordinator/tools/distance/test_classify.py`). 44 is probably fixed by `d846e3644`; it is in the Investigate group because a CastError on nested arrays may remain.
3. **Notes that tell the repair history.** Over all open rows, 162 of 439 name at least one of these: a batch or rung (84 rows), a skeptic, judge or gather (63), a repair design (41), a repair story (26) (`form-signals.txt`). On 2026-10-08 the archaeology found 81% to 88% of era B to D rows naming a batch, so the rework cut this a great deal. What remains is concentrated in the rows that batches note: 577 is the extreme, a log of every batch's sighting. 731 carries another row's correction. 59, 307 and 665 tell what was fixed when.
4. **A reproducer that does not reproduce.** In 731, 313 and 330 the reproducer is a plain test that passes, and in 731 it tests the fixed sibling. A reader takes the cell as the defect's test.
5. **Rows written since the rework are in the best shape** (12 of 19 Keep). The template works for new text, but those rows also start near the limit (section 4).
6. **The era-A rows that hold are the parser and library rows whose code no one has touched** (5, 84, 94, 35, 112, 207). The era-A rows that fail sit where batches 13 to 20 worked: overloading, reductions and inference (20, 44, 97).

## 6. Recommendation

### 6.1 A full pass: needed

- **What it covers.** Every open row, all 439 (about 529K characters of row text, about 170K tokens to read). Read the 117 `POSITIVE-VERIFIED` rows too if the budget allows: they were not sampled.
- **Why every row.** Of the 16 sampled rows that a signal flags, 14 need action, but 9 of the 23 sampled rows that need action carry no signal. So a pass over the flagged rows alone would miss most of the work.
- **What it does to each row.** It applies the rubric of section 5, with this ledger's checks:
  - the claim states what fails now, and names no fixed half;
  - the reproducer reproduces the claim (an `XXX` test while the spec settles it);
  - the notes hold the mechanism with a pinned line, the workaround and the siblings, and no repair story;
  - FACTS and POSITIONS agree with the row.
- **Its size, by the sample's rates.**
  - Flagged rows: 60 × 14/16 ≈ 53. Unflagged rows: 379 × 9/27 ≈ 126. About 180 rows in all need a change. With 27 unflagged rows sampled, the range is roughly 120 to 250.
  - Of these, about 2 in 23 are a close owed, 4 in 23 need a re-measurement (Investigate: about 30 to 40 rows, a later run, not part of the reading), and the rest are a rewrite of the claim or the notes.
  - The 40 rows with refused notes are part of the 180: their notes' texts are in the batch records, so the writer can start from them.
- **Order.** First the routes (6.2). Then the 10 template rows and the 2 owed closes (642, 577). Then the 60 flagged rows, then the rest by section. A reader who knows Fortress but not the batches checks the rewritten rows, as the rubric asks.
- **Not part of it.** Running the 237 `none` rows again. The pass lists the rows whose evidence is too old to trust (Investigate), and a later probe runs them. It does not move rows between sections.

### 6.2 Tool routes before the pass

These are review-queue item 165's routes, which the pass cannot do without. Every gather since climb batch 15 has met these limits.

1. **`ledger.py rewrite N FILE`.** It writes a whole new line for an open row, checked by the template, and keeps the old line in the history ("rewritten"), as `record.py set` does for FACTS. The full pass writes through it, and so do the template fixes and claim corrections such as items 182 and 187. A `--base` check already proves that no text is lost.
2. **`close` for a `CONTESTED` row whose question is settled (642), and for a fix whose test lies outside the test folders (577).** For the second, either accept a test under `explorations/coordinator/tools/`, or accept `--test none` with a reason.
3. **`note` inserts before the "full text: history, row N" marker,** not after it (17 rows show the result). It should lint only the cells it changes, so that a template failure elsewhere in the row does not block a note.
4. **Optional: `lint_spec` reads `library/apis/NAME.tex` as typeset from `NAME.fsi`** (section 2).

### 6.3 Checks at each landing

All of these run on the landing's diff and the ledger, with no build. The synthesis review asks for no full audit after every landing, so these checks look only at the rows that the landing touches. They would have caught 642, 535, 577, 307, 665 and the 40 rows with refused notes when each happened.

1. **`ledger.py check` with a zero allowance.** Run it on the whole ledger, and also `check --base <the batch's base>`. The gather fails on any new failure: batch 12's gather noticed row 642's failure and landed it anyway (`climb-batch-12/RECORD.md:54`).
2. **Renamed or deleted `XXX` tests.** For every `XXX` file that the landing deletes or renames (`git diff --name-status -M BASE..HEAD | grep XXX`), each row that names it in any cell must be closed or rewritten in the same landing. Use `ledger.py find --cites` or a grep for the stem. This catches promotions such as 642, 535, 307 and 665.
3. **Rows that a landing commit names.** List every row named in the landing's commit messages with a repair word, or in a subject as "(row N)". Each must be closed, or its notes changed, in that landing (as for 642 and 577). `scripts/signals.py`'s `commit_signals` does this over a range.
4. **No refused note left over.** The gather's "Ledger notes not written" list must be empty, or each of its items must go through a route of 6.2 before the routing ends. Today 117 refused texts wait in the batch records, and 40 open rows have one that never went in (`scripts/refused_notes.py`).
5. **Rows on the files the landing changes.** For each original-tree file in the diff, `ledger.py find --cites FILE` lists the open rows that cite it, and the record pass reads them by the rubric. This is the "affected related entries" step that the synthesis review gives for FACTS, applied to the ledger.
6. **FACTS and POSITIONS.** For each entry the landing changes, list the rows it names, and compare their statuses. An entry that calls a FIXED row open, as F-174 does row 159, is a finding.

Size budget, for the curator to choose: write a new row at 900 characters at most, so that it can take later notes. 43 of the 92 new open rows began near the limit.

Why: the clause does no work for the compiled checker, whose count of errors in the one library and distance to the switch-over are 0 with it and without it; and a vector or matrix of a program's own complex numbers needs it gone, since the library bounds `Vector` and `Matrix` by `Number` and `MultiplicativeRing`.

- P-66 **The integer principle: Java's and the JVM's defaults stay where they make sense, and are corrected where they fail high performance or mathematical precision.** The team did so with rounding. A hardware behaviour that bytecode can express gets its own explicit spelling, as the specification's wrapping and saturating operators do. Where the JVM prevents a correct implementation, the project gives way for now. The peers to compare are Julia, X10, Swift and Rust.
- P-67 **`round` on an exact half goes to the even integer, on both paths.** Under walk and on the compiled path, `round(2.5)` gives 2: an `RR64` or `RR32` value rounds an exact half to the even integer, as a rational does. This is the specification's rule for rationals, the default rounding of IEEE 754, and the rule of the team's own `round` on rationals.
- P-68 **On the float types, `floor` and `ceiling` return the same float type, while the brackets ⌊x⌋ and ⌈x⌉, `round` and `truncate` return `ZZ`, the unbounded integer.** So `floor(2.5)` is the `RR64` value 2.0, and ⌊2.5⌋ is to be the `ZZ` value 2. - P-69 **`LSHIFT` and `RSHIFT` are bit operators on the fixed-width integer types, and `ZZ`'s `shift` is exact.** On `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `NN32` and `NN64`, a shift loses the bits that it shifts out, silently, as in every peer language. A count at or beyond the width gives 0, or -1 for `RSHIFT` of a negative value, and a negative count shifts the other way, as Swift's and Julia's shifts do. The count may have any integer type, and the shift works at the width of the value shifted. On `ZZ`, the unbounded integers ℤ, `shift(x, k)` is ⌊x·2^k⌋ at any count; there the specification defines `x LSHIFT k` as `shift(x, k)` and `x RSHIFT k` as `shift(x, -k)`. On the compiled path, a shift of a fixed-width value works on the JVM's `int` or `long`, never through `ZZ`. Why: a shift through `ZZ` costs speed wherever the JVM cannot remove it. Row 442: the compiled `NN32` and `NN64` shifts, refused today. Row 383: `ZZ`'s `shift`, which the compiler's prelude does not declare. Row 381: a count of another integer type, where the compiled path refuses a `ZZ`, `NN32` or `NN64` count and computes a `ZZ64` count on a `ZZ32` at 64 bits.
- P-70 **`GCD` and `LCM` give nonnegative results, and `LCM` raises `IntegerOverflow` when the multiple does not fit its type.** So `0 GCD -4` is 4 and `1 LCM -5` is 5, and on `ZZ32`, `(2^31 - 1) LCM 2` raises. The rule applies on both paths. Why: the specification says that both results are nonnegative, and its general rule raises `IntegerOverflow` for an integer result that does not fit. The same general rule makes `GCD` raise it where the divisor does not fit, as in the specification's example `-2^31 GCD 0` on `ZZ32`. Row 442: `GCD` and `LCM` on the compiled path's `NN32` and `NN64`.
- P-71 **An overflow guard tests for the type's most negative value, not for `a = -a`, so `|0|`, `-0` and `0 DIV -1` do not overflow.** On a signed fixed-width type, only the most negative value overflows when it is negated, taken in absolute value or divided by -1. On the compiled path, the natives of negation, absolute value and division on `ZZ32` and `ZZ64` test for the most negative value. The same faulty test sat in `ZZ64`'s multiplication, through which its `REM`, `MOD`, `GCD` and `LCM` compute, so `0 · 5`, `3 REM 5` and `12 GCD 18` raised; that multiplication now raises only when the exact product does not fit. Why: no reading of the specification makes the three cases overflow.

A value that the narrower type holds is unchanged; any other becomes the value of the narrower type with the same low 32 bits. Why: the team's specification said nothing on `narrow`, and the team's boundary test `ProjectFortress/tests/UnsignedTest.fss` asserts the low 32 bits for `NN64` values. On the unsigned types, keeping the low bits is a bit operation, like a shift, and the signed `narrow` gets the same answer.

- P-74 **Mixed integer widths convert by declared coercions: each wider integer type declares a `coerce` from each narrower integer type, as the compiler prelude does.** A conversion that is exact is implicit, and a conversion that can lose precision is written out. So `ZZ32` values and integer numerals coerce into `RR64` implicitly, and a `ZZ64` value into `RR64` is written out (P-66, Java's defaults corrected where they lose precision). A call of a generic function with arguments of mixed widths infers, on both paths, the narrowest type into which its arguments coerce. A range is over `ZZ32` only (P-77, the rule on ranges). The specification's `widens` declaration, which would make a narrow computation stored into a wide variable run wide, is deferred. The implicit coercion of `NN32` into `RR64`: P-75 holds it, with its conflict with the overloads of `RR64` and `ZZ64`.
- P-75 **`NN32` coerces into `RR64` implicitly, since every `NN32` value converts to `RR64` exactly.** Why: a conversion that fits is implicit, the rule of P-74 on mixed widths. With the coercion, an operator that both `RR64` and `ZZ64` declare is ambiguous on both paths for a `ZZ32` with an `NN32`, since neither `ZZ64` nor `RR64` coerces into the other. Without it, P-74's rule, the narrowest type into which both arguments coerce, gives `ZZ64`. Row 575: the coercion, which the tree lacks, with this conflict and its measurement. Each way to build it changes a decided behaviour, so the choice of a way is not a worker's (`fortress-repo`'s exploring part).
- P-76 **An integer numeral has a type of its own, `IntLiteral`, which each number type converts from: in the interpreter's library now, and under walk once walk has the checker's static types.** The design is the compiler's prelude's working one, taken in place of the specification's numeral types, which the team left unfinished. Why the split: walk has no static types, so it would give a list of numerals the element type `IntLiteral`, with no declared type to go by. The interpreter's library declares `IntLiteral`, the conversions from it into the five integer types, `QQ` and `RR64`, and `IntLiteral`'s own arithmetic, which the team had left commented out until coercion existed. Walk still gives an integer numeral the type `ZZ32`, or `ZZ64` or `ZZ` when its value does not fit, so no numeral reaches `IntLiteral`'s declarations under walk. Walk gaps: a numeral that walk matches as a `ZZ32
- P-77 **Scalar ranges are over `ZZ32` only, as the compiler's prelude declares them (`Library/CompilerLibrary.fsi`).** Why: a JVM array has at most as many elements as the largest `ZZ32`. A range over another integer type is a static error. A loop whose counter needs a wider type runs over a `ZZ32` range and widens each element, as in `j: ZZ64 = i`. A range of rank 2 or 3 is a tuple of `ZZ32` scalar ranges. The public range traits, such as `Range[\I\]`, stay generic in their index type: the ranges of rank 2 and 3 extend them at pairs and triples of `ZZ32`.
